recent_posts.title: Modern SID chip substitutes
recent_posts.summary: The Commodore 64's SID sound chip is no longer manufactured but remains highly sought after. Two modern replacements exist: the open-source SIDkick Pico (using a Raspberry Pi Pico microcontroller) and the ARM SID. The SIDkick Pico requires assembly with header pins, firmware flashing, and has separate audio output pins for best quality, though a solder jumper can route audio through the standard pin. The ARM SID offers true plug-and-play compatibility with the original chip's form factor. Both replacements run on 5V only (eliminating the original's 12V requirement) and produce sound quality comparable to the original chip.

recent_posts.title: The SID: Classic 8-bit sound
recent_posts.summary: A detailed walkthrough of interfacing the classic SID (Sound Interface Device) chip from the Commodore 64 with a custom 6502 breadboard computer. Covers the chip's architecture including three independent synthesizer voices, waveform generation (triangle, sawtooth, square, noise), ADSR envelope control, and address decoding logic. Demonstrates practical implementation through register manipulation to generate different sounds and concludes with playing ported music that showcases the chip's capabilities using only basic waveforms and effects.

recent_posts.title: How do aircraft systems communicate?
recent_posts.summary: A detailed exploration of the ARINC 429 protocol used for aircraft system communication, demonstrated through replacing a mechanical altimeter with an electronic one. The piece walks through differential signaling, bipolar return-to-zero encoding, noise resistance through twisted pair wiring, and practical oscilloscope analysis of real avionics data transmission. Shows how modern backup instruments automatically sync with primary flight displays through serial communication protocols.

recent_posts.title: Sound synth with a 6502
recent_posts.summary: A detailed walkthrough of building a sound synthesizer using a 6502 microprocessor breadboard computer. The project demonstrates how to generate different waveforms beyond basic square waves by implementing variable duty cycles through interrupt-driven timer control. The tutorial covers hardware modifications including interrupt wiring with diodes, assembly programming for interrupt handlers, and the use of low-pass filters to approximate triangle and sawtooth waves from square wave outputs.

recent_posts.title: Computer noises
recent_posts.summary: A detailed walkthrough of implementing sound generation on a 6502-based computer using square waves. The tutorial covers using the 6522 VIA chip's timer functionality to generate square waves on pin PB7, amplifying the signal with an LM386 audio amplifier, and creating a BASIC command for playing tones. The implementation includes frequency calculation for musical notes, duration control, and demonstrates playing simple melodies through programmed sequences.

recent_posts.title: Reverse engineering Microsoft BASIC
recent_posts.summary: This post details the process of modifying Microsoft BASIC to enhance its LCD print functionality on a custom-built 6502 computer. It explains how to change the LCD print instruction to handle entire strings instead of individual character codes, highlights the significance of various subroutines, and delves into understanding and manipulating zero page variables. Additionally, it explores floating point representation and offers practical examples including handling string literals and numeric expressions.

recent_posts.title: Hacking Microsoft BASIC
recent_posts.summary: The post details the process of running Microsoft BASIC on a breadboard 6502 computer, focusing on using built-in peek and poke commands to interact with hardware. It explains how to display data on an LCD module directly from BASIC by modifying the language to include new commands. Key steps include peeking and poking to manipulate memory addresses, setting up the LCD in 4-bit mode, and writing assembly code to handle new commands for LCD interaction in Microsoft BASIC.

recent_posts.title: RS232 flow control
recent_posts.summary: The post explains the challenge of managing data flow in a breadboard computer with a limited input buffer. It discusses the use of RS232 flow control, specifically the CTS (Clear to Send) and RTS (Request to Send) signals, to manage the flow of data and prevent buffer overflow. By connecting the CTS pin and enabling RTS/CTS flow control in the terminal, the computer can manage data transmission effectively. The implementation includes correcting hardware bugs and reassigning control signals to ensure proper functioning, allowing large programs to be pasted accurately without missing characters.

top_posts.title: How assembly language loops work
top_posts.summary: The post discusses troubleshooting and optimizing a 'Hello World' project on a self-built 6502 processor-based computer. The initial issue arose when upgrading to a 1 MHz oscillator, causing the LCD to miss instructions due to its processing delay. The post explains how adding delay using no-op instructions partially resolved the problem. Ultimately, checking the LCD's busy flag before sending further instructions provided a more efficient solution. It highlights how to implement this in assembly language, ensuring the system works properly even with the faster clock speed.

top_posts.title: Binary to decimal can’t be that hard, right?
top_posts.summary: Converting a binary number to decimal involves breaking down the number into separate digits using arithmetic operations that a computer can handle, such as addition and subtraction. The process includes rotating bits, subtraction, and managing carry bits to simulate division in binary, which is computationally efficient. The explanation includes an example of implementing this in assembly code on a simple computer, demonstrating how to print out the result in decimal format through detailed steps and loops.
